w: Imre Steindl's neo-Gothic pile on the Pest bank has been Hungary's largest building since it opened in 1902 - a cupola borrowed from a Viennese church, a silhouette borrowed from Vienna's own city hall. Still the seat of the National Assembly, still ruling the Danube skyline.
s: Neo-Gothic giant that's ruled Hungary's skyline since 1902
_facts: Designed by Imre Steindl, neo-Gothic, opened 1902
Largest building in Hungary since completion
Influenced by Vienna City Hall and the Maria vom Siege church cupola
Seat of the National Assembly, on Kossuth Square, Pest side

w: The first permanent span across the Danube, opened in 1849 and named for the count who bankrolled it, though everyone just calls it the Chain Bridge. English-designed, Scottish-built, its cast-iron decorations once counted as a marvel of modern engineering - Budapest's original showpiece crossing.
s: Budapest's first permanent Danube crossing, since 1849
_facts: Designed by William Tierney Clark, built by Adam Clark
First permanent bridge across the Danube in Hungary, opened 1849
Named for Istvan Szechenyi, decorations of cast iron
Regarded as a marvel of modern engineering at the time

w: Seven Magyar chieftains on horseback flank a column at the end of Andrassy Avenue, backed by a colonnade of national leaders cast by sculptor Gyorgy Zala. The stone at its foot gets mistaken for a tomb of the unknown soldier; in 1989 it hosted the reburial of reformist leader Imre Nagy.
s: Seven chieftains, a colonnade of leaders, one reburial
_facts: Millennium Monument with statues of the Seven Chieftains of the Magyars
Memorial Stone of Heroes, often mistaken for Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Hosted the reburial of Imre Nagy in 1989
Most sculptures by Gyorgy Zala

w: Hungary's largest church holds an unlikely relic behind glass: the mummified right hand of King Stephen I, the country's first monarch. Consecrated in his name, it now doubles as co-cathedral of the Esztergom-Budapest archdiocese, and its dome still tops the Pest skyline.
s: A saint-king's mummified hand, under a Pest dome
_facts: Named for King Stephen I, whose right hand is housed in the reliquary
Largest church in Budapest, third largest in Hungary
Co-cathedral of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest

w: An eclectic-neoclassical hall raised opposite Heroes' Square between 1900 and 1906 to house Hungary's international art - over 100,000 pieces, from Egyptian antiquities to Old Master paintings, much of it inherited wholesale from the Esterhazy and Zichy family estates.
s: 100,000 pieces of inherited old-master and antique art
_facts: Built 1900-1906 by Albert Schickedanz and Fulop Herzog, eclectic-neoclassical style
Collection of over 100,000 pieces of international art
Collection built from Buda Castle, Esterhazy and Zichy estate donations

w: A 2.5km sliver of parkland midriver, once called the Island of Rabbits and once a cluster of medieval convents - their ruins still sit among the trees. Three separate islets were stitched together in the 19th century to tame the Danube's flow, and Budapest has been strolling the result ever since.
s: The Island of Rabbits, stitched together from three islets
_facts: 2.5km long island in the Danube, mostly landscape parks
Medieval ruins recall its role as a religious centre in the Middle Ages
Formerly called Insula leporum, Island of Rabbits
Formed from three separate islands joined in the late 19th century

w: Built for the 1896 Millennium Exhibition and originally named for Emperor Franz Joseph, this Art Nouveau span carries mythological sculptures and the national coat of arms on its ironwork. Battered in the war, it was the first bridge rebuilt afterward - and one pillar hides a small museum of the city's bridges.
s: An Art Nouveau bridge with a bridge museum inside it
_facts: Originally named Ferenc Jozsef hid (Franz Joseph Bridge)
Built for the Millennium World Exhibition, Art Nouveau design with mythological sculptures
First bridge rebuilt after WWII damage
Northeastern pillar-house contains a museum on Budapest's bridges

w: Named for an empress assassinated in 1898, whose bronze statue still stands at its Buda end. The original flamboyant 1903 bridge was blown apart in the war; what rose in its place by 1964 was a stripped-back brutalist span, spared any of the old ornament, crossing the Danube's narrowest point in the city.
s: An empress's bridge, rebuilt bare after the war
_facts: Named after Elisabeth of Bavaria, assassinated in 1898, statue at Buda end
Original eclectic flamboyant bridge built 1897-1903, destroyed in WWII
Rebuilt as a simplified brutalist span 1961-1964
Spans the Danube's narrowest point in Budapest, 290m

w: Budapest's grand public park packs in a thermal bath, a zoo, a scatter of 19th-century follies, and a wave of brand-new museums including the Museum of Ethnography. One green square doing the work of half a dozen separate attractions.
s: A park with a spa, a zoo and a museum wave inside it
_facts: Public park close to Budapest's centre, contains 19th-century buildings
Includes Szechenyi thermal bath and Budapest Zoo
New museums built in the early 2020s, including the Museum of Ethnography

w: A three-way bridge with an odd kink: the short spur onto Margaret Island was tacked on two decades after the main span opened in 1876, once the money finally showed up, so the two sections meet at an ungainly 165 degrees. French-engineered, and still the second-oldest crossing in the city.
s: A Danube bridge with a 165-degree afterthought
_facts: Designed by French engineer Ernest Gouin, built 1872-1876
Second-oldest public bridge in Budapest
Spur to Margaret Island added later, meeting main span at 165 degrees
607.5m long, links Buda and Pest plus Margaret Island

w: Europe's largest medicinal bathhouse, fed by twin springs running at 74 and 77 degrees Celsius straight out of the ground. The water carries enough sulfate, magnesium and metaboric acid to count as medicine - Budapest just calls it a very hot swim in City Park.
s: Europe's biggest bathhouse, fed by 77-degree springs
_facts: Largest medicinal bath in Europe
Water supplied by two thermal springs at 74C and 77C
Contains sulfate, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, metaboric acid, fluoride

w: Named for the shipyards that once lined its banks, this is the biggest island in Budapest's stretch of the Danube - a quiet year-round park for eleven months, and one of Europe's biggest music festivals for the twelfth, when the Sziget takes it over every August.
s: A shipyard island that becomes a festival every August
_facts: Largest Danubian island in Budapest, named for former shipyard companies
Located in District III, popular recreational area year-round
Home of the international Sziget Festival every August
